title: Grammatical gender
explanation: French nouns are masculine or feminine, and the article (le/la, un/une) has to agree.
bridge_note: A lot of Portuguese cognates share gender (a mesa, o sol) — but not always: la mer is feminine while o mar is masculine, a real mismatch, not just an exception to memorize away.

title: Negation wraps around the verb
explanation: Standard negation uses two particles, ne before the verb and pas after it — the verb sits inside the negation, not after it.
bridge_note: Portuguese just puts não once before the verb (eu não entendo) — no wrapping. This is one of the real differences, not a shortcut.

title: The subjunctive mood
explanation: Triggered by doubt, wish, emotion, necessity, and certain conjunctions (bien que, pour que, avant que).
example_native: Il faut que tu sois à l'heure.
example_gloss: It's necessary that you be on time.
bridge_note: This uses the same logic as Portuguese "é preciso que você seja pontual" — should feel the most instantly familiar, since English subjunctive barely survives ("I insist that he be present" is close to all that's left of it).

title: Certain common adjectives go before the noun
explanation: A specific, memorizable set (grand, petit, bon, jeune, vieux, beau, nouveau, a few others) front the noun instead of following it.
bridge_note: Portuguese defaults to noun-then-adjective (uma casa pequena), so this is a genuine placement rule, not a free transfer.

title: Adjective agreement
explanation: French adjectives agree in gender and number with the noun they describe.
example_native: Il est grand. Elle est grande.
example_gloss: He is tall. She is tall.
bridge_note: Same underlying concept as Portuguese (alto/alta) — just different endings to learn.

title: Object pronouns generally sit before the conjugated verb
explanation: Unlike English, French object pronouns come before the verb they attach to, not after it.
example_gloss: I you see = I see you.
bridge_note: Lighter touch on this one — Portuguese pronoun placement varies enough by register and region that it isn't a clean one-to-one, flagged as "similar tendency," not a strong claim.

title: Nouns almost always need an article, even in general statements
explanation: French uses an article before a noun even when talking about something in general, not just a specific one.
example_gloss: I like coffee. (literally: I like the coffee)
bridge_note: Portuguese does the same thing (eu gosto do café/eu gosto de café varies), so this one transfers more easily than it does from English, which drops the article entirely for general or uncountable nouns ("I like coffee," no "the").

title: Plural is usually silent on the noun — the article carries it
explanation: The written -s that marks plural is almost never pronounced, so spoken French tells singular from plural mostly by the article, not the noun's ending.
example_gloss: the cat / the cats (chat and chats sound identical)
bridge_note: Portuguese pronounces its plural -s, so the ear can rely on the noun itself. In French the article (le vs les) is doing the work the noun ending does in Portuguese — worth retraining the ear to listen there instead.

title: Everyday past tense is built with avoir/être + past participle
explanation: The passé composé — the tense used for most spoken past-tense statements — is formed with a helper verb (avoir or être) plus the past participle, not a single conjugated past-tense verb form.
example_gloss: I ate an apple. (literally: I have eaten an apple)
bridge_note: Portuguese has a simple one-word past tense (comi) for exactly this everyday use, so the two-part French construction can feel like overkill for something plain and finished — but in French it's the default, not a special "have done" nuance like English's present perfect.

title: y and en replace whole prepositional phrases with one word
explanation: The pronouns y (a place, or "about/to it") and en ("of/from it," or an unspecified quantity) stand in for an entire preposition + noun phrase, placed before the verb like other object pronouns.
example_gloss: I'm going there. / I want some (of it).
bridge_note: Portuguese doesn't compress a prepositional phrase into a single pronoun this way — it tends to just repeat or drop the phrase (vou lá / quero um pouco). French's y/en are a genuinely new compact tool, not a direct swap for anything already familiar.
